items.title: On-field coach: How injury torment gave Kenny a unique outlook for finals bid
items.snippet:
On-field coach: How injury torment gave Kenny a unique outlook for finals bid
Panthers hooker Mitch Kenny has declared he is ready to make up for lost time throughout the finals series after making a successful return from a five-month injury lay off.
The forward broke his leg in
items.body_excerpt:
On-field coach: How injury torment gave Kenny a unique outlook for finals bid
Panthers hooker Mitch Kenny has declared he is ready to make up for lost time throughout the finals series after making a successful return from a five-month injury lay off.
The forward broke his leg in Penrith's Round 7 win over the Dolphins, the injury triggering a lengthy recovery process that challenged him both physically and mentally.
Kenny made a long-awaited return to the field in last week's win over the Tigers and he's emerged as the Panthers wildcard leading into Sunday's final against the Roosters at CommBank Stadium.
Kenny: Grateful to play out the cobwebs
"It's been a long time coming and I wasn't a great watcher of the team those last few weeks," Kenny said. "I've been needing to get back out there so it felt good to do it on a day we honoured John Farragher and secured the minor premiership.
"I wanted nothing but success while I was out and really enjoyed watching Billy Scott debut and Freddy Lussick made the position his own and did a tremendous job for us.
"I'm grateful to be back on the field, to get a game before finals and be trusted by Ivan to go straight back into the team means a lot."

Kenny was initially facing an 8-12 week layoff before a setback in the recovery process delayed his return further and he ultimately spent 20 rounds on the sidelines.
While he'd have preferred to be on the field, the hooker had the chance to watch the game from a different perspective and even received an early taste of what it takes to be an NRL coach.
"I would have rather been playing but everything happens for a reason and there's always a silver lining," Kenny said. "It was an opportunity to look at the game a bit differently and learn about a different side of the game while also giving my body time to freshen up.
"I am interested in coaching but it was pretty stressful watching games with Ivan in the coaching box. I've had the pleasure of being around Ivan, who's going to go down as a legend, and blokes like Peter Wallace and Ben Harden so it was a great environment to learn off those guys."
Kenny will start at hooker on Sunday afternoon, with Billy Scott likely to inject energy off the bench as was the case last weekend. Lussick has also been named on the six-man bench, giving Cleary options with his forward rotations.
With so much talent spread across the park, Kenny has the skills to unlock the players around him as the Panthers look to kick off their finals campaign with a win.
Jenkins: 'You're always an equal' in this team
While he's only been back on the park for one game, the hooker's teammates have already noticed the impact of his return.
"He's had a bumpy road through it all but it hasn't shown," veteran forward Scott Sorensen said. "He's turned up every day with a positive headspace and a positive attitude and he's quite a character within our team.
"We value that and he's brought that every day while he bided his time and done the work. I'm very proud of him and happy he's returned to the field."

items.title: Finals 'Our biggest motivation': Top four sides out to follow proven path to premiership
items.snippet:
'Our biggest motivation': Top four sides out to follow proven path to premiership
The prospect of a Suncorp Stadium preliminary final is driving the Dolphins as they look to take a big step towards a maiden NRL premiership.
Kristian Woolf's men will travel to Auckland to play the
items.body_excerpt:
'Our biggest motivation': Top four sides out to follow proven path to premiership
The prospect of a Suncorp Stadium preliminary final is driving the Dolphins as they look to take a big step towards a maiden NRL premiership.
Kristian Woolf's men will travel to Auckland to play the first final in the club's history on Saturday afternoon and they are determined to ensure it's the last time they hit the road before the grand final.
It's the same path the Broncos took to last year's decider, Reece Walsh inspiring a stunning comeback over the Raiders before a thrilling preliminary final victory over the Panthers at a sold-out Suncorp Stadium.
Warriors v Dolphins: Finals Week 1
History shows teams that win a qualifying final in the opening week of the post-season have a much greater chance of playing in the grand final and Dolphins captain Tom Gilbert said his side is determined to swing the odds in their favour this weekend.
"To have the chance to play a preliminary final at our home stadium is our biggest motivation," Gilbert told NRL.com. "It's the same for them, they'll want that as well so there's a lot of motivation there for both sides.
"If we think too far ahead we won't get this weekend right so we're looking forward to the opportunity and challenges that comes with playing in New Zealand and we're going to try enjoy the week."
The top four sides will do battle on either side of the Tasman this weekend, with a week off and a place in the preliminary final on the line.
The Warriors will host the Dolphins at Go Media Stadium on Saturday afternoon before the Panthers take on the Roosters in a CommBank Stadium blockbuster on Sunday.
Gilbert's blessing in disguise
The winners will enjoy a rest while the losers will be thrust into a sudden-death semi-final against the two elimination final winners next weekend.
Statistics provided by rugby league historian David Middleton reveal just how important a win is this week for the four teams contesting qualifying finals.
In every season since the NRL introduced the current finals format in 2012 at least one qualifying final winner has gone on to play in the grand final.
On the flipside, just four top four teams have lost in week one and recovered to progress to the decider.
The 2015 Cowboys and 2021 Panthers are the only two sides to lose a qualifying final before reeling off three-straight victories to claim the premiership.
While they did it the hard way in 2021, Penrith took the more direct route in 2022, 2023 and 2024 by winning in week one and enjoying a week off before the preliminary final.
Panthers v Roosters: Finals Week 1
Having experienced both paths, veteran forward Scott Sorensen said it's crucial his side opens their finals campaign with a win.
"I'm not going to deny how important it is to start the finals on the front foot and perform well," Sorensen said. "You build confidence in that and then have the luxury of a week off to freshen up.
"If we have to do it the hard way or the easy way, we're just as prepared.
"It is tougher if you have to go out there and play for another 80 minutes but at the end of the day, if you lose and want to get there, that's the way you've got to go. You've got to accept it, move on and be excited for the occasion."

items.body_excerpt:
'Go out there and express myself': Hugo ready to rise to challenge
Daly Cherry-Evans was brought to Bondi for one reason - to help the Roosters win a premiership.
With halfback Sam Walker ruled out with an ankle injury, the 37-year-old’s quest for a fairytale finish to his decorated career rests on a halves combination that has barely had the chance to develop.
Cherry-Evans will partner 24-year-old Hugo Savala in the Roosters’ qualifying final against Penrith on Sunday, with the pair having started just two games together in the halves all season.
It is a far cry from the combination Cherry-Evans had built with Walker, which helped steer the Roosters to fourth on the ladder with 16 wins from 24 games.
But rather than viewing their minimal experience in the halves together as a weakness, Cherry-Evans sees a golden opportunity.
“Once we were aware of the Sam situation, we have been training a lot together, so there’s a lot of reps done together,” Cherry-Evans said.
No half measures for Savala
“I watched Hugo playing in the halves last year and really admired the way that he went after it, the style of footy that he plays.
“There’s a lot of skill in it, but there’s a really tough mentality. He attacks the game physically as well, so I’m really excited to play alongside him and I feel like we’re able to complement each other out there.”
Savala has played 40 NRL games and spent much of this season becoming one of Trent Robinson’s most valuable utilities - doing a job at centre, five-eighth, halfback and off the bench, and bagging eight tries along the way.
DCE preparing for one last NRL Finals charge
With the season on the line, he is back in his preferred role, wearing the No.6 jersey alongside one of the most experienced halfbacks the game has produced.
“We don’t need him to be Sam, we need Hugo to be Hugo,” Cherry-Evans said.
“Hugo’s got a very, very strong career ahead of him in the halves.”
Savala knows exactly what his role will be as he and DCE match motors with Panthers champion Nathan Cleary and the ever-reliable Jack Cole.
“Obviously Chez will play the senior role, be the traditional seven, but I’ll still have my input too,” Savala said.
“I’ll play my style and my football. We’ve got a good system in place here at the Roosters, so I can slot in there and play my role.
“It’s a great opportunity to go out there and express myself and be myself.”
Hugo Savala just fires wherever he's put
Savala has had the box seat this season to see how the veteran conducts himself at training and on game day, learning from the way he communicates and controls the team around him.
“Probably a lot of stuff outside of football, the person he is and the way he conducts himself on the field and at training and the little parts of his game,” Savala said.
“He’s been big for me with the vocals and communication, how he gets the boys around the park. It’s been really key for me.”
Related Finals
Free public transport ensuring finals fever takes over Sydney
And Cherry-Evans has loved learning from Savala and Walker in return.
Which was part of the reason he left Manly after 15 seasons, to continue challenging himself and learn from the next generation of playmakers.
“I have learned so much from my teammates and the coaching staff here, and Hugo and Sam have certainly taught me about the game of rugby league.
“Once you feel like you know everything about the game, it’s probably time to retire.”
Cherry-Evans will wrap up his NRL career at the end of the season before moving to the Super League, and these finals could provide the perfect fairytale ending, or leave him wondering what might have been.
Daly Cherry-Evans celebrates milestone game in style
“If my legacy doesn’t come down to these remaining three to four games then I probably haven’t done enough for the last however many I have played,” he said.
“To finish your career in the NRL as an NRL premiership winner, that would be as good as it gets.
“But I know life doesn’t just give out fairytales.

items.body_excerpt:
History lesson: Last time the contenders met in a final
A whole new competition starts this weekend as eight contenders go into battle across four matches in three days with one goal in mind.
The Panthers have proven themselves the masters of finals football across the past five years while the Roosters (2002, 2013, 2018, 2019), Sharks (2016), Cowboys (2015), Rabbitohs (2014) and Knights (2001) all have premierships to their name in the NRL era.
The Dolphins are in their first ever finals series and their opponents the Warriors have been here 10 times but never come away with a title.
With two sudden-death showdowns and two qualifying finals coming up this weekend, NRL.com takes a look at the most recent September clash between the sides.
Knights v Rabbitohs
2020 elimination final
The Rabbitohs and Knights have only met once in finals football, and it came in exactly the same circumstances as Friday night at Allianz Stadium.
Six years ago, South Sydney and Newcastle finished sixth and seventh respectively before meeting in a sudden-death elimination final.
Now, with the Rabbitohs sixth and the Knights seventh again, history is repeating itself as the two sides prepare to do battle for a place in the semi-finals.
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that 2020 clash.
Match Highlights: Rabbitohs v Knights
Alex Johnston, Campbell Graham, Cody Walker, Tevita Tatola and Cameron Murray were all part of the Rabbitohs side that night six years ago, while Dane Gagai, who will now wear a Knights jersey, also featured for South Sydney.
Newcastle has just three players remaining from that team in Kalyn Ponga, Bradman Best and Jacob Saifiti.
And if Friday night follows the script from 2020, South Sydney will be hoping for a repeat of the result.
The Rabbitohs blew the Knights away 46-20, with Johnston crossing twice alongside Tatola, two names who will again feature in the elimination final six years later.
Alex Johnston finds the line during the Bunnies' 46-20 win over the Knights in the 2020 elimination final.
Roosters v Panthers
2024 qualifying final
The Roosters and Panthers know each other all too well when it comes to September football.
Their last three finals meetings have all come in the qualifying final, and once again, they find themselves in exactly the same position.
Their most recent showdown came in 2024, when Penrith began its march towards a fourth straight premiership with a commanding 30-10 victory over the Roosters at BlueBet Stadium.
Panthers v Roosters – Finals Week 1, 2024
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that clash, with the Panthers’ champion core and the Roosters’ star-studded spine preparing to renew one of the competition’s fiercest finals rivalries.
Penrith has won four of its past five finals meetings with the Roosters, but with a preliminary-final spot and a precious week off on the line, history will count for little when these two heavyweight clubs collide again.
Yep, he's back!
Sharks v Cowboys
2024 semi-final
The Sharks and Cowboys have plenty of finals history, and their most recent meeting could provide the perfect blueprint for another high-stakes showdown.
The two clubs have met six times in finals football, with the teams splitting those matches at three apiece but it was the Sharks who had the last laugh.
Sharks v Cowboys – Finals Week 2, 2024
When the sides met in the 2024 semi-final at Allianz Stadium, Cronulla held on for a 26-18 victory to book a place in the preliminary final and end the Cowboys’ campaign.
Braydon Trindall played a starring role that night, scoring twice, and now, two years on, he’ll return from injury with another chance to make his mark.
This time, there is no second chance.
With both sides fighting to keep their premiership dreams alive, Saturday afternoon’s clash promises another chapter in a finals rivalry that has produced plenty of drama over the years.

items.body_excerpt:
Marky Mark making every moment count in run to the finish
Mark Nawaqanitawase knows his time in the NRL is quickly running out.
The Roosters winger will return to rugby union next season, leaving him with just a handful of NRL games remaining, and he is determined to make every one count.
The 26-year-old’s NRL career has been short but certainly not short of highlights.
In just two seasons, Nawaqanitawase has represented NSW twice, played three Tests for Australia, and finished as the NRL’s leading tryscorer in 2025 with 24 four-pointers.
Now, as he prepares for his second NRL finals campaign, there is an added emotion to every training session and every game.
“Simply just coming into training every day, I’m trying to soak it all up and enjoy every moment. I’m going to miss it," Nawaqanitawase said.
Yep, he's back
“The realisation that it’s gone quite fast, so just trying to enjoy every minute.”
But there is little time for sentiment when the Roosters’ premiership campaign is on the line.
After finishing fourth, Trent Robinson’s side will face Penrith in a qualifying final on Sunday at Commbank Stadium, with a win sending them straight through to a preliminary final.
For Nawaqanitawase, simply reaching September is no longer enough.
DCE preparing for one last NRL Finals charge
“A good feat to get to the finals, but it’s actually doing something in the finals, which is what I want to do this year,” he said.
And there could hardly be a tougher opening assignment.
Nawaqanitawase’s aerial ability has been one of his biggest weapons since switching codes but he knows gun playmaker Nathan Cleary will be launching all manner of high balls on Sunday.
“We need to be ready for anything he does,” he said.
Nawaqanitawase talks Panthers clash
“We do a little bit of study here and there, but on Sunday it could change and he could do something different.”
Nawaqnitawase will also have his hands full defensively, with Penrith’s Tom Jenkins - one of the competition’s most dangerous finishers, with 30 tries in one season so far.
But Nawaqanitawase is up for the challenge.
“I’m looking forward to coming up against him,” he said.
“I mostly focus on what I can do for the team and going out there and making sure we can get the win.
“It will be a challenging day for our edge, it's going to be a tough game, and everyone has got to be on."

items.title: Injury returns, Roosters form, Panthers unstoppable?: The FIVE biggest questions for the NRL finals - Zero Tackle
items.snippet: Injury returns, Roosters form, Panthers unstoppable?: The FIVE biggest questions for the NRL finals    Zero Tackle
items.body_excerpt:
After 27 weeks of the NRL competition, the cream has risen to the top with eight remaining to fight for the premiership trophy on the first weekend of October.
With plenty of sides showing strengths and vulnerabilities in recent weeks, intriguing questions emerge of who will make the significant moves during the play-offs series?
Here are the five biggest questions heading into Week 1 of the finals.
5. Are the Warriors finally ready to win the whole competition?
The Warriors have grown as the season has continued. Injuries crept in, didn't matter. They stuck to their system, and the next man came in and did a job. It is full credit to Andrew Webster for recruiting incredible depth, which has separated the contenders from the fake.
They face the prospect of playing two home finals before packing their bags for Accor Stadium, and shape up as the most formidable road trip out of the teams left fighting in the competition.
With a lethal forward pack, led by Mitchell Barnett and James Fisher-Harris , balanced with Erin Clark's ball-playing and offloads, and a damaging interchange one-two punch with Demitric Vaimauga and Tanner Stowers-Smith , they simply roll other forward packs off the field.
AUCKLAND, NEW ZEALAND - MARCH 13: The Warriors celebrate after Roger Tuivasa-Sheck of the Warriors takes a conversion during the round two NRL match between New Zealand Warriors and Canberra Raiders at Go Media Stadium, on March 13, 2026, in Auckland, New Zealand. (Photo by Phil Walter/Getty Images)
The stars are aligning for the Warriors to do something magical in the next month of the season, but must take care of the Dolphins first and foremost.
If they can stiffen up their edges, which have resulted in leaking 30+ points in the past fortnight, they are on the doorstep of bringing home their first ever NRL premiership.

Panthers vs Roosters Preview & Betting Tips: 2026 NRL Qualifying Final
September 12 th 2026, 6:03pm , By: Ben Bridge
Sunday afternoon at CommBank Stadium delivers a heavyweight qualifying final between the minor premiership winning Panthers and a Roosters side that has already proven this season it can beat Penrith at this exact venue. The stakes are simple: the winner earns the week off and progresses directly to a home preliminary final, while the loser survives but faces a sudden death semi-final in Week 2.
Penrith enter their seventh consecutive finals series chasing a fifth premiership in six seasons, while the Roosters have qualified for September for the 10th consecutive year. These are two clubs entirely comfortable at this stage of the season.
The Panthers deserve favouritism, particularly after reclaiming the minor premiership in Round 27, but I do not want to lay a considerable number against this Roosters side. The Roosters beat Penrith 12-6 at CommBank Stadium less than a month ago, producing one of the defensive performances of the season.
Sam Walker being ruled out is a significant blow, but the Chooks return almost every other major player rested in Round 27. James Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Reece Robson, Lindsay Collins, Victor Radley, and others all return, while Angus Crichton has been named on the bench after 11 matches out with a foot injury.
This matchup screams close finals football.
Panthers vs Roosters Prediction & Tips: 2026 NRL Qualifying Final
Panthers Reclaim Their Place at the Top
Penrith’s regular season was another demonstration of why this dynasty has endured even as the personnel around the club continues to change. They started 2026 at a frightening pace, winning 11 of their first 12 matches, absorbed a difficult post Origin period and ultimately recovered to claim the JJ Giltinan Shield in the final round.
Their ability to survive without stars was arguably the defining feature of the year. In Round 13, Penrith faced the Warriors without Nathan Cleary, Isaah Yeo and Brian To’o yet still won 20-18 in a high-quality contest where both teams completed above 89 per cent. That ability to maintain their systems despite missing elite players is what continues separating Penrith from almost every other club.
Now the important pieces are largely back.
Yeo returns to the starting side for his second match after a pectoral injury, allowing Lindsay Smith to return to prop. Dylan Edwards is at fullback, Cleary controls the side from halfback, Mitch Kenny starts at hooker and the forward pack includes Moses Leota, Isaiah Papali’i and Liam Martin. Scott Sorensen also returns to the bench after being rested in Round 27.
That spine gives Penrith an enormous game management advantage in finals football. Cleary can control territory better than anyone in the NRL, Edwards gives them relentless yardage and support play, while Yeo’s return restores the middle link that makes their attack so difficult to read.
The Panthers have not been invincible. Their middle part of the year contained several losses, and the Roosters exposed them at CommBank Stadium in August. But Penrith’s ability to grind through poor periods remains unmatched.
There is also the Ivan Cleary storyline sitting in the background after the mid-season announcement that he will step down following 2027. It has not distracted the team from winning another minor premiership, and if anything, the final two seasons of this remarkable era now carry additional urgency.
The Panthers have been here repeatedly. That experience is their biggest advantage this weekend.
Roosters Enter September as Genuine Threat
The Roosters may have finished fourth, but their regular season was far better than that ladder position alone suggests.

items.title: The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future? - SMH.com.au
items.snippet: The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future?    SMH.com.au
items.body_excerpt:
In the “before time” of four weeks ago, when Sam Walker still roamed the field without a moon boot, the Roosters were premiership favourites.
As James Tedesco notes, you don’t exactly forget “the best defensive performance of your season”.
The Tricolours’ stirring 12-6 upset of Penrith on August 13 wasn’t just their most recent victory. It was the club’s biggest win in years, finally shaking the chokehold Ivan and Nathan Cleary had held them in – to the tune of an 11-1 record – in the six-again era.
They rattled Nathan like never before, regularly rushing up on the champion No.7 given Isaah Yeo was sidelined, shutting down Penrith’s attack with goal line defence (occasionally illegal) that harked back to their halcyon 2018-19 premiership-winning days.
Ten days later, the Roosters lost to the Tigers . They’re still yet to fully recover.
Walker went down the following week against the Dolphins, and Trent Robinson chose to cut his losses and rest nine of his best players for the local derby against the Rabbitohs, which they lost by 30.
That Panthers breakthrough capped an eight-game winning run, in which they conceded a miserly 12.8 points a game (the best record of any side over that period).
The rhythm that went out the window in a bludging Sunday afternoon, 25-24 loss to the Tigers briefly returned against the Dolphins a week later.
But both losses were set up by alarming defensive lapses – the kind Penrith have taken and beaten teams senseless with for years now.
The Roosters coughed up three tries between the 19th and 26th minutes to the Tigers – two down their right edge and another directly from a fumbled pass on their own line.
The Roosters were premiership favourites just a month ago. NRL Imagery
The Dolphins peeled off three tries in nine minutes before half-time, targeting Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia’s suspect decision-making on the Roosters’ left.
“When things don’t go our way, we’ve struggled to get back to what we do well,” Tedesco says – having been sidelined (and rested) for all bar the Dolphins game in the past month.
“We can’t let things snowball, and in those games, one bad thing has led to another. So I think that’s on me as captain and the leaders to help fix that up against Penrith. Things aren’t always going to go perfectly. But you can’t let that slide for 15-20 minutes either. You have to move onto the next job and recover.”
How the Roosters’ attack recovers without the enigmatic Walker and adjusts to the probable scrum-base combination of Daly Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala is key.
“Maybe they become a little more structured,” champion playmaker and ex-Roosters halves coach Cooper Cronk says.
“Maybe they [adopt] a little bit more of a set-play mentality – play one, two, three [settling plays] and then play off the back of that.
“Sam Walker’s effectiveness is his unpredictability. Maybe the Roosters narrow that down a bit and start doing a little bit of sequence play to get the best out of Savala and Cherry-Evans.”
The returns of Victor Radley (concussion) and Daniel Tupou (back last week from a lengthy shoulder injury) can’t be overstated.
Can Daly Cherry-Evans get the Roosters’ campaign back on track? James Brickwood
The Roosters attack was the definition of clunky against the Tigers. Without Radley holding them together in the middle, and then understandably when rocked by Walker’s injury, they were listless for much of the Dolphins clash too.
For all their attacking wares, the Roosters haven’t been that flash attacking from inside the opposition’s 20-metre zone all season.
But the 43 tackles they had pressing the Tigers’ line, and 38 doing the same from inside the Dolphins’ 20, should have been enough to win both matches by their standards.
The Roosters have still scored the most tries from kicks (33) of any team this season. But of late, one of their best attacking weapons has been holstered – Rex Bassingthwaighte’s 79th-minute try against the Rabbitohs last week was their first from the boot in a m

items.title: Dolphins down Warriors 26-16 to reach preliminary finals
items.snippet: The Dolphins are through to the NRL preliminary finals after defeating the Warriors 26-16 last night.The Dolphins ran in four ...
items.body_excerpt:
[Image: Dolphins]
The Dolphins are through to the NRL preliminary finals after defeating the Warriors 26-16 last night.
The Dolphins ran in four tries to one to etch their name in the history books.
Selwyn Cobbo, Herbie Farnworth, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and Jack Bostock scored a try apiece for the Queensland side.
Meanwhile, the Warriors have another chance to qualify for the preliminary finals, as they will face the Newcastle Knights next weekend.
In another result last night, the Sharks beat the Cowboys 26-16.
The Sharks will take on the loser of the Panthers and Roosters match.
Coming up today, the Panthers will meet the Roosters at 6.05pm.
